Learning outcomes
  1. Identify the degree, coefficients, and constant term of a polynomial.
  2. Apply different methods of factoring polynomials.
``` - Factorization is the process of rewriting a complex algebraic expression as a product of simpler expressions known as **factors** (the product of these factors, when multiplied, is equal to the original expression) as shown in @fig-factors. - This technique is used for solving equations and evaluating limits. ![Factorization of an algebraic expression](/images/factors3.png){#fig-factors fig-align="center" width="400"} ## Factorization of polynomials ### Polynomials {#polynomials} - A polynomial in one variable can be written as: $$ a_nx^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1x+a_0 $$ **where**: - $\displaystyle a_n, a_{n-1}, ..., a_1, a_0$ are constants referred to as the polynomial **coefficients**: - The leading coefficient (the coefficient of the highest power) $a_n\ne 0$. - $\displaystyle a_0$ is referred to as the **constant term** that can be considered as $a_0x^0$. - The highest power ($n$) in the polynomial is known as the **degree of the polynomial**. - Based on the degree, the polynomial can be classified as: - Cubic polynomial, if the degree is three ($n=3$). - Quadratic polynomial, if the degree is two ($n=2$). - Linear polynomial, if the degree is one ($n=1$).

### Methods of factoring polynomials #### Greatest common factor - This method is based on factoring out the greatest common factor (GCF) from the terms of the polynomial. - The GCF is the largest expression that divides each term of the polynomial without leaving a remainder. - For example, the GCF of $9x^2 + 3x$ is $3x$. ```{=html}
Worked Examples & Practice
``` :::: panel-tabset ## Example M.3.1 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Factor: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{10x^3 + 6x^2 - 2x}$ - The largest integer that divides every coefficient ($10, 6, 2$) is $2$, and the highest power of $x$ that divides every term (alternatively said, the lowest power of $x$ that appears among the terms) is $x$, so the **GCF** is $2x$: $$ 10x^3 + 6x^2 - 2x = \boxed{2x(5x^2 + 3x - 1)} $$ ## Example M.3.2 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Factor: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{24x^4y^2 - 60x^3y^3 + 36x^2y^4}$ - This is an example of a multivariable polynomial (i.e., there are two variables, $x$ and $y$); the same method still applies. - The largest integer that divides every coefficient ($24, 60, 36$) is $12$, the lowest power of $x$ that appears among the terms is $x^2$, and the lowest power of $y$ that appears among the terms is $y^2$, so the **GCF** is $12x^2y^2$: $$ 24x^4y^2 - 60x^3y^3 + 36x^2y^4 = 12x^2y^2(2x^2 - 5xy + 3y^2) $$ - The quadratic expression in the parenthesis can be factored further into two binomials $\Rightarrow (2x - 3y)(x-y)$. This method will be covered in the following sections (refer to the section [quadratic expressions](#qdr-poly)). - So, the complete factorization of the above expression becomes $\Rightarrow \boxed{12x^2y^2(2x - 3y)(x-y)}$. ## [Exercise M.3.1 {{< iconify fluent:chat-bubbles-question-20-filled size=21px >}}]{style="color: #ba181b"} What is the **GCF** for the expression: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{18x^3y - 30x^2y^2 + 12xy^3}?$ - The **GCF** is ::: #### The difference of two squares - A binomial with the form $x^2 - y^2$ can be factored to $(x + y)(x - y)$ ```{=html}
Worked Examples & Practice
``` ::: panel-tabset ## Example M.3.3 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Factorize: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{x^2-9}$ $$ x^2-9 = \boxed{(x+3)(x-3)} $$ ## Example M.3.4 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Factor: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{16y^2-49x^2}$ $$ 16y^2-49x^2= (4y)^2-(7x)^2= \boxed{(4y+7x)(4y-7x)} $$ ## [Exercise M.3.2 {{< iconify fluent:chat-bubbles-question-20-filled size=21px >}}]{style="color: #ba181b"} Factor: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{25a^2-81b^2}$ - The answer is ::: #### Quadratic expressions {#qdr-poly} - A quadratic expression is a polynomial of degree 2. - Its form is $ax^2+bx+c$, where $a\neq 0$ (this is equivalent to the general polynomial notation $a_2x^2+a_1x+a_0$). - Some quadratic expressions can be factored into two linear binomials with real number coefficients. However, those with a negative discriminant ($b^2-4ac$) cannot be factored into linear factors over the real numbers. - **If the coefficient** $a = 1$: - Find two numbers ($n_1$ and $n_2$) whose product is the constant $c$ ($n_1 \times n_2 = c$) and whose sum is the coefficient $b$ ($n_1 + n_2 = b$). - The numbers $n_1$ and $n_2$ can be positive or negative, depending on the signs of $b$ and $c$. - The quadratic expression can be then factored to $(x+n_1)(x+n_2)$. - **If the coefficient** $a \ne 1$: - Calculate $a\times c$. - Find two numbers (e.g., $b_1$ and $b_2$) that their product is equal to $(a\times c)$ and their sum gives the coefficient $(b)$. - Replace the term $bx$ with the terms $b_1x$ and $b_2x$. - Group every two terms and simplify by taking a common factor. - Simplify further by taking one parenthesis as a common factor. ```{=html}
Worked Examples & Practice
``` ::: panel-tabset ## Example M.3.5 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Factor: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{x^2-3x-10}$ - $a=1,\ b=-3,\ c=-10$. - The discriminant is $(-3)^2-(4 \times 1 \times -10)=49$, which is greater than $0$, so the expression can be factored into two linear factors with real coefficients. - We need to find two numbers whose product is $-10$ and whose sum is $-3$. - The product of $-5$ and $2$ equals $-10$ and their sum equals $-3$, so this expression can be factored to $\Rightarrow \boxed{(x-5)(x+2)}$. ## Example M.3.6 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Factor: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{2x^2-7x-15}$ - $a=2,\ b=-7,\ c=-15$. - The discriminant is $(-7)^2-(4 \times 2 \times -15)=169$, which is greater than $0$, so the expression can be factored into two linear factors with real coefficients. - $a\times c=2\times -15=-30$. - The two numbers whose product is $-30$ and whose sum is $-7$ are $-10$ and $3$, so $b_1 = -10$ and $b_2 = 3$. - So, the above expression can be written as $\Rightarrow 2x^2-10x+3x-15$. - Group the first two terms and the last two terms together, so the expression can be written as $\Rightarrow (2x^2-10x)+(3x-15)$. - Factor out the common factor from each parenthesis, so the expression can be written as $\Rightarrow 2x(x-5)+3(x-5)$. - Simplify further by taking $(x-5)$ as a common factor, so the expression can be factored to $\Rightarrow \boxed{(2x+3)(x-5)}$. ## Example M.3.7 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Factor: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{x^2+x+1}$ - $a=1,\ b=1,\ c=1$. - The discriminant is $1^2-(4 \times 1 \times 1)=-3$, which is less than $0$, so the expression cannot be factored into linear factors with real coefficients. - This expression can be factored using complex numbers but this topic is out of the scope of this refresher, so we I will not cover it here. ::: #### Cubic polynomial factorization ##### Cubic binomial - A cubic binomial is a polynomial with two terms and degree three ($x^3 + y^3$). - It can be factored using the sum or difference of cubes formulas: - $x^3 + y^3 = (x + y)(x^2 - xy + y^2)$ - $x^3 - y^3 = (x - y)(x^2 + xy + y^2)$ ##### Long or Synthetic division for cubic polynomial - If one root $r$ (i.e., a value of $x$ that makes the polynomial equal to zero) of the cubic polynomial is known, long or synthetic division can be used to divide the cubic polynomial by $x - r$. - The quotient will be a quadratic polynomial, which can then be factored further. - These methods are not covered here, but for technical details refer to [Math is Fun](https://www.mathsisfun.com/algebra/polynomials-division-long.html) for long division or [BYJU'S](https://byjus.com/maths/synthetic-division/) for synthetic division. ## References -
